steps.action:
The Last Evening Beacon

When Captain Elias Finch first arrived on Driftwood Isle, the lighthouse stood like a lonely sentinel, its granite tower weather-blasted and streaked with salt. The townsfolk said the building was older than any living memory, built when whales still outnumbered ships. Elias, once a merchant-navy officer, had come seeking stillness after years of storms that raged outside and inside him alike.

Each night he climbed the 132 spiral steps, lit the great Fresnel lens, and coaxed it into its slow, glittering rotation. The beam swept past slate cliffs, over black water, and into the open vastness where ships lurked beyond the horizon. That pulse of light—every eight seconds—was his heartbeat.

Life on the island was quiet, but not silent. Seals barked on the shoals at dawn. The radio crackled with distant voices. And once a week, Mara the mailboat pilot brought letters, tins of sardines, and, occasionally, stories of the mainland: new factories, electric streetcars, rumors of automated lights that needed no keeper.

“Someday,” Mara said, leaning over the rail, “they’ll put a clockwork lamp up here. You could come back to town.”

Elias only smiled. The sea had taught him that nothing man-made ran forever—not engines, not fortunes, not even grief. Best to tend the flame while you could.

One autumn night, a fog deeper than any he’d known rolled in, swallowing the island whole. The horn moaned its warning, and the sea answered with a roar. Beyond the shroud, a freighter named Rose of Galway was limping north, her compass lost to a lightning strike. Elias radioed, but static hissed. All he had was the beam.

He trimmed the wick, stoked the lamp, and watched the lens whirl. Suddenly the mechanism coughed, gears grinding. The light faltered. Kerosene dripped where it shouldn’t. In the dark glass he saw his reflection—an aging man, shoulders slumped like tired sails. But beyond the pane, he imagined sailors scanning the murk, praying for that eight-second heartbeat.

Elias seized the crank, muscles straining, and forced the lens to turn by hand. Minutes bled into hours. Smoke stung his eyes, sweat iced his back. Once, he thought he heard a distant bell—a ship’s buoy or a chapel in a dream. He wouldn’t let the light die.

Just before dawn, the fog thinned. Low on fuel, the lamp guttered, but its final sweep caught a black hull veering toward jagged rocks. A single degree of change was all the Rose needed. Her silhouette slid past the reef and into open water.

Exhausted, Elias slumped beside the cold lantern, lungs tasting soot and salt. Outside, gulls screamed at the rising sun. He listened for the freighter’s whistle, but none came; perhaps gratitude is silent, carried on the wind.

Weeks later, Mara brought news: the Rose of Galway had reached Halifax, her captain sending thanks to “the invisible hand that turned night into morning.” Mara also carried official papers: the Coast Office would soon automate Driftwood Light. No keeper required.

Elias signed where they pointed, then climbed the 132 steps one last time. He polished the brass, wiped soot from the lens, and whispered goodbye to gears that had trusted his heartbeat.

That evening, as the supply boat hummed away, an electric bulb flickered on, sterile and steady. But out on the horizon, beyond the reach of clocks and circuits, the ocean kept its own memory. And if you stood on Driftwood Isle after twilight, you might still feel it: every eight seconds, a pulse like a stubborn echo of a man who, for one endless night, kept the world from breaking on the rocks.
